Central Nervous System
Histology
CEREBELLUM & CEREBRUM

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the histological structure of the cerebellum and the cerebrum. The cerebellar cortex has three layers (molecular, Purkinje cell, granular) overlying a white-matter medulla that carries the afferent and efferent fibers and contains the cerebellar nuclei. The cerebral cortex has six layers built mainly from pyramidal and granule-type neurons, and is responsible for learning, memory, sensory integration, and initiation of motor responses.

Cerebellum

General organization

  • The cerebellum is formed of two hemispheres joined by the median vermis.
  • Its surface is thrown into many folds, the folia, giving a tree-like appearance.
  • Each folium has an outer cortex (grey matter) and an inner medulla (white matter).

Cerebellar cortex: three layers (outside to inside)

LayerCellsFibers / key connections
Molecular (outer) Few cells: outer stellate neurons and basket cells, plus neuroglia Mainly fibers: Purkinje dendritic arborization, granule-cell axons (and their bifurcation), climbing fibers, axons and dendrites of stellate and basket cells
Purkinje cell (middle) A single layer of large multipolar pyriform Purkinje cells Dendrites branch richly in the molecular layer; axons enter the white matter and terminate around the cerebellar nuclei
Granular (inner) Closely packed small granule cells and Golgi cells Mossy-fiber terminals (rosettes), climbing fibers passing to the molecular layer, and Purkinje cell axons

Molecular layer

The most superficial layer. It contains mainly nerve fibers with few nerve cells and neuroglial cells.

Fibers present

  • Dendritic arborization of the Purkinje cells.
  • Axons of the granule cells and their bifurcation.
  • Climbing fibers from the olivocerebellar pathway.
  • Axons and dendrites of the stellate and basket cells.

Cells present

  • Outer stellate neurons: small cells in the outer part of the layer. Their processes are confined to the molecular layer, and their axons make synaptic contact with Purkinje cell dendrites.
  • Basket cells: lie in the deep part of the layer. Their dendrites synapse with granule-cell axons and climbing fibers. Their axons run horizontally just above the row of Purkinje cells and make basket-like contacts with several Purkinje cells.

Purkinje cell layer

  • Made of one layer of large multipolar, pyriform nerve cells.
  • Dendrites are highly branched in the molecular layer.
  • Axons enter the white matter and terminate around the cerebellar nuclei.

Granular layer

Composed of closely packed small cells that look like granules. Two cell types are present:

  • Granule cells: rounded cells with deeply stained nuclei and a very thin rim of cytoplasm, each with a few short dendrites inside the granular layer. Their dendrites synapse with excitatory mossy fibers (from the pontine nuclei). Their T-shaped axons pass to the molecular layer, where they form hundreds of thousands of synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites.
  • Golgi cells: resemble Purkinje cells, except that their dendrites fan out in a different plane in the molecular layer. Their axons are confined to the granular layer and synapse with granule cells, giving them inhibitory feedback.

Three kinds of fibers are found in this layer: terminals of mossy fibers (expanded as mossy-fiber rosettes), climbing fibers passing to the molecular layer, and the axons of Purkinje cells.

Key distinction: mossy fibers excite granule cells (granular layer), whereas climbing fibers go to the molecular layer and synapse directly with Purkinje cell dendrites.

Cerebellar white matter (medulla)

Afferent fibers

  • Mossy fibers: come from different parts of the CNS and end around the granule cells.
  • Climbing fibers: come from the inferior olive and terminate in the molecular layer, synapsing with Purkinje cell dendrites.
  • Recurrent collaterals: arise from Purkinje cell axons and end on the dendrites of Golgi cells.

Efferent fibers

The efferent fibers are the axons of the Purkinje cells.

Cerebellar nuclei

  • Masses of grey matter embedded in the cerebellar white matter.
  • They are cell stations that receive the axons of Purkinje cells and relay the impulses to the vestibular nuclei and the red nucleus.
  • The nuclei are the dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial nuclei.

Cerebrum

General organization

  • The cerebrum consists of two large hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum.
  • Each hemisphere has a surface layer of grey matter (the cerebral cortex) and a central white matter that contains the basal ganglia.
  • The surface carries sulci and gyri, which divide it into functional areas.

Cerebral cortex: six layers (outside to inside)

The cortex is formed of nerve cells, nerve fibers, and blood capillaries arranged in six layers. In addition to neurons, it contains supporting neuroglia: astrocytes, oligodendroglia, and microglia.

#LayerContents
1MolecularFew scattered spindle-shaped neurons (horizontal cells of Cajal) lying parallel to the surface, glial cells, and nerve fibers
2External granularSmall multipolar (stellate) neurons and small pyramidal cells
3External pyramidalMedium-sized pyramidal neurons and neuroglial cells
4Internal granularThin layer of closely arranged small granule (stellate) cells and neuroglia; greatest cell density of the cortex
5Internal pyramidalThe largest pyramidal cells (cells of Betz) and neuroglia; long apical dendrite extends toward the molecular layer; lowest cell density of the cortex
6MultiformNeurons of various shapes and sizes: fusiform and polygonal neurons with few short dendrites (cells of Martinotti)

Density contrast: the internal granular layer (4) has the highest cell density, while the internal pyramidal layer (5) has the lowest.

Function of the cerebral cortex

The cerebral cortex is responsible for learning, memory, sensory integration, information analysis, and initiation of motor responses.

Key Points / Quick Review

Cerebellum: organization

  • Two hemispheres + median vermis; surface folded into folia.
  • Each folium: outer grey cortex, inner white medulla.

Cerebellar cortex (outer to inner)

  • Molecular: mainly fibers; outer stellate and basket cells.
  • Purkinje cell layer: one row of large pyriform cells.
  • Granular: granule cells and Golgi cells.

Cerebellar cell connections

  • Basket cell axons form baskets around several Purkinje cells.
  • Granule cells receive mossy fibers; their T-shaped axons synapse with Purkinje dendrites.
  • Golgi cell axons stay in the granular layer and inhibit granule cells.

Cerebellar fibers and nuclei

  • Afferents: mossy fibers, climbing fibers (from inferior olive), Purkinje recurrent collaterals.
  • Efferents: Purkinje cell axons.
  • Nuclei: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial; relay to vestibular nuclei and red nucleus.

Cerebrum: organization

  • Two hemispheres linked by the corpus callosum.
  • Surface grey cortex; central white matter containing basal ganglia.

Cerebral cortex layers (outer to inner)

  • 1 Molecular; 2 External granular; 3 External pyramidal; 4 Internal granular; 5 Internal pyramidal; 6 Multiform.
  • Layer 4: highest cell density. Layer 5: lowest density, Betz cells.
  • Cells of Cajal in layer 1; cells of Martinotti in layer 6.
  • Functions: learning, memory, sensory integration, analysis, initiation of motor responses.
